semantics.note: The proposition matches the statement. It is framed as an observation, but it turns on the evaluative word 'proper'.

contract.note: The contract rightly finds that 'proper' has no agreed standard. Any verdict would depend on a measure the speaker never gave.

evidence.note: A June 2025 preprint showing that cognitive-map methods existed but were imperfect. It cannot decide whether such methods count as 'proper'.

reviews.rationale: Whether the methods available in mid-2025 count as 'proper' ways to build symbolic world models on the fly is the speaker's own judgment, and he gives no measure. MindCube-style map-then-reason methods existed but were imperfect, which neither confirms nor refutes the claim. The claim is too evaluative to score.

attribution.note: Marcus's own assertion. Chollet is quoted separately and is not part of this claim.

semantics.note: A firm observation that tool use improves performance. Dropping 'abundantly clear' leaves the commitment itself unchanged.

contract.note: The plain reading (executable tools improve correctness on the reasoning and algorithmic tasks discussed, not every model on every task) is ordinary and fits the context.

evidence.note: OpenAI's own disclosure reports near-perfect Python-enabled AIME scores and says tool use improved benchmark results. The packet gives no no-tool baseline, so this support is weak.

An independent June 2025 preprint: o4-mini failed River Crossing without tools and solved it with Python. GPT-4o's failure with tools shows the gain is not universal, but there is no systematic deterioration.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows tool-enabled then-current models doing better on reasoning and algorithmic tasks. There is an independent controlled puzzle comparison, plus OpenAI's own report of tool-driven benchmark gains. GPT-4o's failure with tools limits any universal reading, but it does not show deterioration. The plain-reading support condition is met, though the evidence base is thin.

semantics.note: 'From what I can tell' marks limited confidence, and the drafter recorded it as 'likely'. The speaker also says implementation details are sketchy. This is hedged, not a firm commitment.

contract.note: The contract scores hedged language on a plain reading, which policy forbids. It also adds a majority census standard and a 'heavy use' threshold that the speaker did not supply.

evidence.note: The DeepSeek-R1 report shows rule-based rewards and correctness-filtered samples for one model family. It says nothing about how widespread this is.
The Qwen3 report shows more synthetic data in training, but does not quantify how much was generated by symbolic rules.

reviews.rationale: The speaker qualifies the claim with 'from what I can tell' and admits details are sketchy. That is graded, limited-confidence language, so it is not scored. Even on the contract's reading, the packet has two model families and no census of models, so it could not settle the claim either way.

Neither shows general elimination. The support condition is met. The flagged mitigation in e2 was explicitly incomplete, so it does not contradict the claim.
